messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Alex, a 38‑year‑old Middle Eastern hairdresser, has lived the past year in a tense limbo since the day a sudden, life‑threatening illness brought him to the edge of death. In a cramped, bright shop on a street that buzzes with the chatter of customers, he has been forced to confront the images of his own fragility. The flash of the hospital photo album that sits on his countertop—images of the white‑washed walls, the metallic instruments, the fluorescent lights—triggers a surge of dread. The sight of those photos instantly sends his heart racing, and the sense of fear and horror that he feels feels all too real. It is as if the room, and the terror that once filled it, has leapt out of the pictures and into his living space. That same picture also brings back the acrid smell of antiseptic that he can still taste when he thinks about the emergency room, and the sharp pain in his chest that the doctor described as “the same pain he felt when the heart stopped.” The photograph therefore does three things at once: it stirs the strong negative emotions that fill his mind, it reminds him that his body is unreliable and feels like an enemy, and it sends him back to the exact sensations he experienced during the crisis. The photo is not only a reminder of the past; it is a trigger that pulls him into the present and makes him feel as if the danger is again looming. The nightmares have taken on a life of their own, too. Every night Alex wakes from a vivid dream in which he is strapped to a machine, the lights flickering, the sterile smell heavy in his lungs. The dream residue is not only frightening; it fuels his belief that the world is untrustworthy. In the mornings he wakes with his heart pounding and his throat tight, convinced that a second, hidden attack is waiting. The physical reactivity that follows—a sudden tremor, a sharp chest ache—makes him think that his own body is betraying him, as if he can no longer trust its signals. The terror that follows is a negative appraisal that “my body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe,” a feeling that has become a core belief in his mind. Because of this, he has stopped going to the quarterly health check‑ups that his employer offers, convinced that the very act of sitting in a chair for a blood test would resurrect the fear that he has already lived. The avoidance is not a mere inconvenience; it is a direct consequence of the belief that the medical procedure itself could be a catalyst for another crisis. The memory of the hospital day itself is vivid, though not always in the form of a clear image. Sometimes, a sudden chill on his skin or a faint taste of antiseptic will flood him with the exact pain he felt in his chest, the same pain that made him clutch his ribs. Other times, he simply feels an intense wave of guilt and shame, as though the illness was his fault, even though he was a patient. The memory is not confined to visual recall; the olfactory trigger and the feeling of pain bring the scene to life, and with that the sense of being in constant alert. These memories are the fuel that feeds the ongoing cycle of dread. When the memory surfaces, it sends him into a state of hyper‑vigilance; the belief that his body is an unreliable weapon keeps him in a state of readiness, and his body’s own reactions—tension in his shoulders, a racing heartbeat—make him think he is already on the brink of another crisis. This creates a self‑reinforcing loop: the memory amplifies his sense of danger, the danger deepens his belief that his body is a threat, and that belief brings the memory back again. The relentless loop has not only consumed Alex’s mental space; it has begun to erode his professional life. He once thrived on the close interaction with clients, their stories, and the rhythmic clacking of scissors. Now, any mention of a doctor’s appointment or a mention of a medical term triggers an immediate collapse of composure. He has avoided clients who ask about health or who show a concern that leads him to speak about the clinic. At home, he keeps his phone to an emergency contact in case he needs to call a doctor, but he rarely picks it up. The avoidance is a protective mechanism, but it also isolates him and reduces his confidence as a hairdresser. He fears that if he is perceived as unreliable—his body betraying him—his clients will leave. The thought that he is “going crazy” because of the symptoms he cannot control is a heavy weight he carries, a belief that is as painful as the physical sensations. Alex finally came to the therapist after a particularly harrowing night when the dream was followed by a day in the shop where a client’s conversation about a recent check‑up made him feel as if the world was suddenly a place of potential harm. He wanted to understand why his body would always feel in danger, why the images of a hospital would trigger not only pain but also a sense that he was no longer in control of his own body, and why he could not simply “shake it off.” He fears that his condition might make him a risk in the salon, and he hopes that learning to untangle the web of memories, triggers, and appraisals will let him regain a sense of safety and control in his own hands.
